newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Germany's Kinkel says EMU must start on time - paper.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kinkel says EMU must start on time - paper.

text.p: Europe's common currency, the euro, should be introduced as planned in 1999 so Europe plays in the world economy's first division, German Vice-Chancellor Klaus Kinkel said on Tuesday in a Swedish newspaper.

"The economic and monetary union is Europe's big answer to the world economy, which is growing together," Kinkel, also Germany's foreign affairs minister, said in a column in Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter.
"It is the core of an extensive future program for the European Union.
"Therefore the euro must be introduced on January 1, 1999, as agreed on in Maastricht. If we do not take that chance, it might not return for several decades.
"The euro is no end in itself. After (establishing) the inner market, the union's economy must quickly be put on another footing, the economic and monetary union (EMU).
"Only if this happens can Europe play in the world economy's first division in the 21st century."
He warned against stimulating the economy through devaluation and inflation as this would lead to a more severe crisis.
"We will not allow ourselves to enter such a vicious circle," he said.
He said an independent central bank and strict interpretation of convergence criteria were necessary to secure a stable currency.
In addition, Germany wants as many countries as possible to join EMU from the start, he said.
"No country that meets stability criteria in the longterm will be excluded from the euro," Kinkel said.
Kinkel added he was convinced of success for the inter-governmental conference, for preparations for the next European Union expansion round and for the planned introduction of the euro.
